127.title: Eid al-Fitr
127.hook: new clothes, the Eid prayer, visiting, sweets, and eid mubarak
127.howItsDone: On Eid al-Fitr, Muslims eat a few dates, wear their best clothes, say takbir on the way to the Eid prayer in a mosque or open ground, listen to the sermon, then spend the day visiting family and friends, sharing food and gifts, and greeting each other with eid mubarak.

segments.voice: Yesterday: zakat al-fitr, the charity of the fast's end, paid before the prayer. Your line was everyone eats on eid. Did you find a way to give one meal's worth? Day one hundred twenty-seven.

It's early morning, and the house smells like cardamom and fried dough. Kids are up before their alarms, pulling on clothes that still have the tags on. Someone eats a few dates standing in the kitchen. On the way out, the whole family is saying something together, over and over: Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar. In a park, or a stadium, or a big hall, thousands of people in their brightest colors line up in rows on the grass. After a month of empty afternoons, today no one is allowed to fast. Today: Eid.
screen: `CARDAMOM AND FRIED DOUGH.` → `CLOTHES WITH THE TAGS STILL ON.` → `TODAY, NO ONE FASTS.`

segments.voice: Eid means a festival. Arabic dictionaries tie it to a root for returning: the day that comes back every year. Eid al-Fitr is the feast of breaking the fast, the first day of the month after Ramadan. And much of what people do on it has a thread back to the Prophet ﷺ. Anas said in Bukhari that the Prophet wouldn't go out on the morning of Eid al-Fitr until he'd eaten some dates, an odd number of them. So the fast is broken first thing, on purpose. It's actually forbidden to fast on the day of Eid. People wash, put on their best clothes, and go out to the Eid prayer, saying takbir along the way. The prayer is two rak'ahs, with extra takbirs, and then a sermon. The Prophet would go to it by one road and come back by another; scholars give several reasons, and one is that more people along the way could greet him. Then comes the visiting, the food, the gifts for children, and the greetings: eid mubarak, a blessed Eid, and an older one reported from the companions, may Allah accept from us and from you. And there's a small story in Bukhari about what the day is for. On an Eid, the Prophet was resting at home while two girls were singing. Abu Bakr came in and scolded them: this, in the Prophet's house? And the Prophet said: leave them, Abu Bakr. Every people has its festival, and this is our festival. Some readers take this to mean the joy isn't a lapse after the serious month, but part of the worship. A month of holding back ends with a day of being glad, together.
screen: `EID — THE DAY THAT RETURNS.` · `DATES FIRST; NO ONE FASTS.` · `ONE ROAD THERE, ANOTHER BACK.` · `LEAVE THEM, ABU BAKR.` · then, large: `THIS IS OUR FESTIVAL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say eid mubarak, or its spirit, to someone. First, sit for a moment, and think back over the month this path has just walked through: the moon, the dawn meal, the date at sunset, the nights, the tongue, the gift. Then think of one person to greet. If they're Muslim, and it's Eid, send them eid mubarak. If not, or if it isn't Eid, send someone a message that's simply glad they exist. Let it be a small feast. The bell holds the time.
Eid. The festival that returns; Eid al-Fitr, the feast of breaking the fast, with dates, the prayer, visiting and sweets. Today's word.
Your line: a blessed feast. Today, take one ordinary meal and make it a small celebration: better plates, someone to share it with, no phone. Day one hundred twenty-seven.

what it means: the festival that returns, where joy is read as part of the worship, and fasting is forbidden.

128.title: The day of Arafah
128.hook: the pilgrims stand on the plain, and others fast the day
128.howItsDone: On the ninth of Dhu al-Hijjah, pilgrims stand on the plain of Arafah from midday to sunset in prayer and supplication, while many Muslims who are not on Hajj fast that day.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Eid, the feast at the end of Ramadan. Your line was a blessed feast. Did you say eid mubarak to anyone, even in a message? Day one hundred twenty-eight.

The month of the pilgrimage, the ninth day. A wide, bare plain outside Mecca, a low hill in the middle of it, and the sun climbing. A crowd of pilgrims reaching past the edge of sight, most of them dressed alike in plain white. Nobody is shopping. Nobody is sightseeing. From noon until sunset, they mostly just stand there, and ask. And far away, in kitchens and offices, other Muslims skip breakfast that morning, because they're fasting the same day. Today: the day of Arafah.
screen: `A BARE PLAIN OUTSIDE MECCA.` → `MILLIONS IN WHITE, STANDING.` → `AND FAR AWAY, A FAST.`

segments.voice: Arafah is the ninth day of Dhu al-Hijjah, the month of the pilgrimage, and it's also the name of the plain itself. The Hajj has many rites: circling the Kaaba, walking between two hills, throwing pebbles, the sacrifice. But the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ summed it up in two words, reported by Tirmidhi and Abu Dawud: the Hajj is Arafah. Miss the standing on that plain, and in the view of the scholars, you've missed the Hajj. The standing is called wuquf. There's no fixed script for it. People pray, recite, weep, ask for forgiveness, ask for their families, in Arabic and in every other language. Tirmidhi reports that the best supplication is the supplication of the day of Arafah. Sahih Muslim adds that there's no day on which Allah frees more people from the Fire. It's a day of history too. Jabir's long account in Sahih Muslim has the Prophet giving his sermon at Arafah, on his farewell pilgrimage. And Bukhari reports that one line of the Qur'an came down on a Friday at Arafah: This day have I perfected your religion for you. Now the other half of the picture. For those at home, the tradition offers the fast. Sahih Muslim reports that fasting the day of Arafah is hoped to wipe away the sins of the year before and the year after. The pilgrims usually don't fast; they need their strength to stand. Many others do. One day, two ways of keeping it: standing on the plain, or fasting at your desk.
screen: `THE NINTH DAY, AND THE PLAIN.` · `THE HAJJ IS ARAFAH.` · `A FAREWELL, AND A FINISHED VERSE.` · `AT HOME: THE FAST.` · then, large: `ONE DAY, TWO WAYS TO KEEP IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give one day's worth of focus. Sit or stand, whichever feels more like the plain. Picture the whole of today, from waking to sleep, as one long afternoon of standing. Now choose one thing you'll give your full attention to today, and only one: a person, a piece of work, a question you keep avoiding. Hold it in mind. If you pray, you can ask for help with it, in any words you have. If not, simply stay with it and let everything else wait. The bell holds the time.
Arafah. The ninth day of the pilgrimage month, and the plain where the pilgrims stand from noon to sunset. Today's word.

Your line: the standing day. Somewhere in today, when you'd normally reach for your phone, stand still for one minute instead, and ask for one thing, or simply notice where you are. Day one hundred twenty-eight.

129.title: Eid al-Adha
129.hook: the feast of sacrifice remembers Ibrahim, and the meat is shared in thirds
129.howItsDone: On the tenth of Dhu al-Hijjah Muslims pray the Eid prayer, and families who can afford it sacrifice an animal, often dividing the meat among the household, relatives and friends, and the poor.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Arafah, the plain where the pilgrims stand from noon to sunset. Your line was the standing day. Did you stand still for one minute, and what did you notice? Day one hundred twenty-nine.

A freezer after a family celebration: foil packets, labeled in marker, stacked up, some of them already promised to other people. In some Muslim homes, the day after Arafah ends a bit like that. It starts with the Eid prayer, early, in new or best clothes. Hugs, and eid mubarak again. And then a very old question: who gets the meat? This is the second of the two Eids, and the end of a run on this path that began with a new moon. Today: Eid al-Adha.
screen: `FOIL PACKETS, ALREADY PROMISED.` → `THE SECOND EID.` → `WHO GETS THE MEAT?`

segments.voice: Eid al-Adha means the feast of the sacrifice. It falls on the tenth of Dhu al-Hijjah, the day after Arafah, while the pilgrims are finishing the Hajj. It remembers a story in Surah as-Saffat. Ibrahim sees in a dream that he is sacrificing his son, and tells him. The son answers: do what you are commanded; you'll find me, if Allah wills, among the patient. They both submit. And at that moment Allah calls out to Ibrahim that he has already fulfilled the vision, and verse one hundred seven says: Then We ransomed him with a tremendous victim. The Qur'an doesn't name the son in this passage. Tradition usually names Isma'il; some early scholars said Ishaq. Either way, the story ends with a life spared. In South Asia and elsewhere, the sacrifice is called qurbani, from the Arabic qurban, which comes from a root meaning to be near. An offering is a way of drawing near. In Arabic it's usually called udhiyah. Families who can afford it sacrifice a sheep, a goat, or a share in a cow or camel, or pay someone to do it on their behalf, often in a poorer country. Scholars differ on how binding it is: the Hanafi school calls it required for those who can afford it; the other major schools call it a strongly recommended sunnah. The Qur'an, in Surah al-Hajj, says the flesh and the blood don't reach Allah; what reaches Him is your devotion. So the meat is for people. The same surah says to eat of it and feed the poor, and a common recommendation divides it in three: a third for the household, a third for relatives and friends, and a third for the poor. A feast that isn't finished until someone who has nothing gets a plate.
screen: `THE TENTH DAY: THE FEAST.` · `IBRAHIM, HIS SON, AND A RANSOM.` · `QURBAN — TO DRAW NEAR.` · `THE FLESH DOESN'T REACH ALLAH.` · then, large: `A THIRD FOR THE POOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: share food three ways. Sit comfortably and picture the next meal you'll make or buy. Now, in your mind, divide it. One part for you and whoever lives with you. One part for someone you know: a friend, a neighbor, a relative you haven't called. And one part for someone you don't know, who needs it. Picture each plate going to its place. Breathe with each one. Then, if you can, decide how one of those three plates will actually leave your kitchen this week. The bell holds the time.
Qurbani. The sacrifice of Eid al-Adha, from a root meaning to be near, its meat shared with family, friends and the poor. Today's word.

Your line: a third for the poor. Today, before you finish anything that's yours, a meal, a paycheck, an afternoon, set a third of something aside for someone who has less. Day one hundred twenty-nine.

130.title: Just ask
130.hook: du'a is asking Allah directly, any time, in any language
130.howItsDone: Muslims make du'a at any time and in any language, often after the salat or with hands raised, asking Allah directly for their own needs and for others.

segments.voice: Yesterday: qurbani, the sacrifice of Eid al-Adha, shared three ways. Your line was a third for the poor. Did one plate, or one third of something, leave your hands? Day one hundred thirty.

For weeks now, this path has been teaching forms. The exact words of the prayer, in Arabic. Where the hands go. How many times to say glory. How many units at dawn. All that precision has a counterweight. There's one kind of prayer in Islam that has no required form at all. No set words. No set language. No set time. You don't even need to be facing anywhere. You just talk. Today: just ask.
screen: `WEEKS OF EXACT FORMS.` → `ONE PRAYER WITH NO FORM AT ALL.` → `YOU JUST TALK.`

segments.voice: The word is du'a, from an Arabic root that means to call, the way you'd call someone's name across a room. The salat, the five daily prayers, is the fixed form: set times, set movements, set words in Arabic. Du'a is the open one. Asking Allah for something, directly, whenever you want. In Arabic, in English, in Urdu, in the half-sentences you'd use at three in the morning. In the usual view, it doesn't need wudu, or a prayer mat, or a particular direction, though people often face the qiblah and raise their hands. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ gave it a surprising rank. Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi report him saying: du'a is worship itself. And then he recited a verse, Surah Ghafir, forty, sixty: And your Lord hath said: Pray unto Me and I will hear your prayer. Not a formal request through the proper office. Pray unto Me. What about the times it seems nothing happens? The hadith collections are honest about that. Bukhari reports that a person's du'a is answered as long as they don't grow impatient and say, I prayed and prayed and nothing came. And a hadith in the Musnad of Ahmad says that a du'a asking for nothing sinful, and not for cutting family ties, is answered in one of three ways: given now, saved for the next life, or a harm of the same size quietly turned away. In that teaching, no such du'a is wasted. It may come back in a shape nobody ordered. Which leaves only the hard part: actually asking.
screen: `DU'A — TO CALL.` · `SALAT IS FIXED; DU'A IS OPEN.` · `DU'A IS WORSHIP ITSELF.` · `ANSWERED IN ONE OF THREE WAYS.` · then, large: `JUST ASK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask for one thing plainly. Sit comfortably. Take a breath, and let it out slowly. Now find the thing you actually want, not the polite version. Maybe it's small: sleep, a good conversation tomorrow, the test results. Maybe it's large. Put it into one plain sentence. If you pray, you can say it to Allah, in any language, out loud or silently. If you don't, just say the sentence to yourself and notice how it feels to admit you want it. Then sit with it, and don't add anything. The bell holds the time.
Du'a. Calling on Allah directly, any time, in any language, asking for what you need. Today's word.
Your line: just ask. Somewhere today, you'll catch yourself worrying about something. When you do, turn the worry into one plain sentence of asking, and leave it there. Day one hundred thirty.

131.title: Hands open
131.hook: hands raised like a bowl, because He is shy to return them empty (Abu Dawud)
131.howItsDone: Many Muslims raise their hands, palms up and held together, when making du'a, especially after the prayer; some wipe the face afterward and some do not.

segments.voice: Yesterday: du'a, calling on Allah in any words you have. Your line was just ask. Did a worry turn into one plain sentence of asking? Day one hundred thirty-one.

Watch a toddler who wants something. They don't write a speech. They stand in front of you with both hands up and open, and wait. It's almost impossible to walk past. Grown-ups do it too, without thinking: palms up when we say, I don't know what else to do. Palms up when we're handed something precious. It's the body saying, I'm not holding anything back, and I'm not grabbing. In mosques all over the world, after the prayer, you'll see people sit and lift their hands in exactly that shape. Today: hands open.
screen: `A TODDLER, BOTH HANDS UP.` → `PALMS UP: NOT HOLDING, NOT GRABBING.` → `AFTER THE PRAYER, HANDS LIFTED.`

segments.voice: Yesterday we said du'a has no required form. That's true. But it has a gesture that many Muslims love: hands raised in front of the chest, palms up, held together a little like a bowl, the way you'd hold them under a tap. Why a bowl? Because a bowl is empty, and it's ready to be filled. The reason comes from a hadith in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi. The Prophet ﷺ said: your Lord is shy and generous. He is shy, when His servant raises his hands to Him, to send them back empty. That's an astonishing thing to say about God. Not stern. Not reluctant. Shy, the way a generous host would be embarrassed to send a guest away with nothing. The Arabic word there, hayiyy, is related to haya, the modesty and shyness that the tradition calls a branch of faith in people. Here it's turned around and said of the Lord. The Prophet's own hands tell the story too. Bukhari reports that when he prayed for rain in a year of drought, he raised his hands so high that the white of his underarms could be seen. It wasn't a polite gesture. It was a whole body asking. Some details differ among Muslims. Some wipe their face with their hands at the end of the du'a, and some scholars say the hadith for that is weak and leave it out. Some raise their hands after every prayer; others save it for particular moments. But the open palm itself is everywhere. It says: I've come with nothing in my hands, and I'm not ashamed of that.
screen: `PALMS UP, LIKE A BOWL.` · `HE IS SHY TO RETURN THEM EMPTY.` · `A WHOLE BODY ASKING FOR RAIN.` · `SOME WIPE THE FACE, SOME DON'T.` · then, large: `I'VE COME WITH NOTHING IN MY HANDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold your hands open for a minute. Sit comfortably. Bring your hands up in front of your chest, palms up, side by side, like a bowl. Let your shoulders drop. Notice the air on your palms. Notice how hard it is not to close them, or fidget, or grab your phone. If you pray, you can hold your du'a in them, silently, and wait. If not, just let them stay open and empty, and notice what it's like to hold nothing. When your arms get tired, rest them on your knees, palms still up. The bell holds the time.
Hands open. The shape of du'a: palms up like a bowl, because the Lord is shy to return them empty. Today's word.

Your line: open hands. Once today, when someone asks you for something, or you feel yourself clenching, turn your palms up, even in your lap, and see if the answer changes. Day one hundred thirty-one.

132.title: "I am near"
132.hook: when my servants ask about Me, I am near, I answer (2:186)
132.tomorrow: Good in this world and the next
132.howItsDone: Muslims often make du'a quietly, with the lips moving and little sound, following 2:186 and the Prophet's teaching that Allah is near and hears.

segments.voice: Yesterday: hands raised like a bowl, because He is shy to return them empty. Your line was open hands. Did you turn your palms up once, and did anything change? Day one hundred thirty-two.

On a bad phone line, people raise their voices. Across a parking lot, they shout and wave. To someone right beside them, in the dark at the end of a long day, they whisper. The volume of a voice carries a guess about distance: how far away the listener is. So here's a question for anyone who has ever prayed, or wanted to: how far away is the One you're talking to? Today: I am near.
screen: `FAR AWAY, PEOPLE SHOUT.` → `RIGHT BESIDE THEM, THEY WHISPER.` → `HOW FAR AWAY IS HE?`

segments.voice: The answer is in Surah al-Baqarah, verse one hundred eighty-six, tucked right in the middle of the verses about the Ramadan fast. And when My servants question thee concerning Me, then surely I am nigh. I answer the prayer of the suppliant when he crieth unto Me. Commentators point to how that verse is built. Elsewhere in the Qur'an, when people ask the Prophet a question, the answer begins with one word: Say. They ask you about the new moons; say. They ask you about wine; say. But here, when they ask about Allah Himself, there's no say. No go-between. The answer comes straight back: I am near. The Prophet ﷺ taught the same thing on a road. Bukhari and Muslim report that on a journey, the companions were calling out Allahu akbar at the tops of their voices. He told them: go easy on yourselves. You're not calling on someone deaf or absent. You're calling on One who hears, who is near, and who is with you. And another verse, in Surah Qaf, puts it even closer: We are nearer to him than his jugular vein. The vein in your own neck. So in Islam you'll often see du'a made quietly. Lips moving, almost no sound. Not because anything is secret, but because you don't shout at someone who's that close. Nearness here isn't a feeling you have to work up. It's a claim the text makes, whether you feel it or not.
screen: `2:186 — THEN SURELY I AM NIGH.` · `NO 'SAY': THE ANSWER COMES STRAIGHT.` · `NOT DEAF, NOT ABSENT.` · `NEARER THAN THE JUGULAR VEIN.` · then, large: `YOU DON'T SHOUT AT SOMEONE THAT CLOSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: whisper, don't shout. Sit comfortably and let your breathing slow down. Notice the pulse in your neck, if you can find it, or at your wrist. Now bring to mind the thing you asked for two days ago, or anything you'd like to ask. If you pray, you can say it, but barely: lips moving, almost no sound, as if to someone sitting right beside you. If you don't pray, whisper it to yourself, just as quietly. Then stop, and stay in the quiet after it. The bell holds the time.
I am near. The answer in Surah al-Baqarah to anyone who asks where Allah is: near, and answering the one who calls. Today's word.
Your line: he is near. The next time you catch yourself thinking, nobody's listening, lower your voice instead of raising it, and say what you need quietly. Day one hundred thirty-two.

133.title: Good in this world and the next
133.word: Good in this world and the next
133.hook: the short du'a from the Qur'an: our Lord, give us good here and good hereafter (2:201)
133.howItsDone: Muslims often recite 2:201, rabbana atina fid-dunya hasanatan, at the end of their du'a, in the prayer, and while circling the Kaaba between the Yemeni corner and the Black Stone.

segments.voice: Yesterday: I am near, the answer that comes with no go-between. Your line was he is near. Did you lower your voice instead of raising it? Day one hundred thirty-three.

Some people, when they finally get the chance to ask for something, ask for too little. Just get me through this week. Others go the other way, and turn it into a grand, dramatic bargain. Both are very human. In Sahih Muslim there's a story about a man who did the dramatic kind. He'd become so sick and thin that, in the report's words, he looked like a baby bird. The Prophet ﷺ visited him and asked what he'd been praying for. His answer was startling. And the Prophet gave him a better one. Today: good in this world and the next.
screen: `TOO LITTLE, OR TOO DRAMATIC.` → `A MAN LIKE A BABY BIRD.` → `THE PROPHET GIVES HIM A BETTER ONE.`

segments.voice: The man said: I've been asking Allah, whatever punishment You'd give me in the next life, give it to me now, in this one. He was trying to get it over with. The Prophet told him he couldn't bear that, and asked him why he didn't say instead the du'a from Surah al-Baqarah, verse two hundred one. Here it is in Pickthall's translation: Our Lord! Give unto us in the world that which is good and in the Hereafter that which is good, and guard us from the doom of Fire. The report says the man prayed it, and Allah healed him. In Arabic it begins rabbana atina fid-dunya hasanatan: our Lord, give us in this world good. The word for good, hasanah, shares its root letters with ihsan, excellence, and husn, beauty. It isn't narrow. Commentators such as Ibn Kathir read good in this world widely: health, knowledge, a good spouse, honest provision. The verse doesn't choose. It leaves the space open. Notice its shape. In the verse just before, the Qur'an describes people who only ask, give us in this world, and stop. This du'a asks for both. Not this life instead of the next, or the next life instead of this one. Good here, and good there. Anas, who served the Prophet, said in Bukhari that this was the du'a he made most often. Abu Dawud reports the Prophet saying it while circling the Kaaba, between two of its corners, and pilgrims say it there still. Some people close their own du'a with it, as a way of asking for everything they forgot to mention.
screen: `PUNISH ME NOW, HE PRAYED.` · `SAY 2:201 INSTEAD.` · `HASANAH — A WIDE WORD FOR GOOD.` · `BOTH, NOT ONE OR THE OTHER.` · then, large: `GOOD HERE, AND GOOD THERE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say it once, in Arabic or English. Sit comfortably, and if you like, raise your hands, palms up. Breathe. If you pray, you can say the verse once, slowly: rabbana atina fid-dunya hasanatan, wa fil-akhirati hasanatan, wa qina 'adhaban-nar. Or in English: our Lord, give us good in this world, and good in the hereafter, and guard us from the Fire. If you don't pray, simply think of one good you want here, and one good you'd want to last beyond it. Hold both at once. The bell holds the time.
Good in this world and the next. The short du'a of Surah al-Baqarah, asking for good here, good hereafter, and protection. Today's word.
screen: `GOOD IN THIS WORLD AND THE NEXT — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: good here, good there. When you catch yourself asking for too little, or bargaining too hard, ask for both instead: something good for today, and something that lasts. Day one hundred thirty-three.
